questions.stem: A refunds MCP tool issue_refund(order_id, amount, reason) is sometimes invoked twice for the same order: once before a client timeout and again when the agent retries. Using the tool_use_id as an idempotency key did not prevent duplicates. Why, and what works?
options: Add 'never refund the same order twice' to the tool description, so the model checks history before calling.
tool_use_id changes on every call; dedupe on a business key such as order and reason, backed by a unique constraint.
Lower the temperature to 0 so the model makes the same decision every time and does not call the tool again.
tool_use_id is reused across retries, so generate a fresh random UUID per tool call and use that as the idempotency key.
questions.explanation: Idempotency keys must identify the intent, not the call. Each tool_use_id is unique, and so is a fresh random UUID (D), so neither deduplicates retries. A business key with a unique constraint makes repeats harmless even under concurrency, and passing it downstream protects against provider-level duplicates. Prompt or temperature changes (A, C) do not control retries.

questions.stem: A client asks you to connect Claude to a 70-document policy library (about 60K tokens total), with no per-user access restrictions, updated twice a year. Questions often require combining clauses from different policies. The client's first instinct is to build a vector database. What do you recommend, and why?
options: A vector database with fine-grained chunking and reranking, since retrieval scales better as the library grows.
Fine-tune a model on the policies twice a year, aligned with the update schedule, so the knowledge is built into the model.
Include the whole library as a cached prefix, since it fits, and revisit RAG if that changes.
One agent per policy, with an orchestrator that consults the relevant agents and combines their answers.
questions.explanation: When the corpus fits comfortably in context, has no access restrictions and changes rarely, full context with prompt caching is simpler and avoids retrieval failures, and it lets the model connect clauses across documents. RAG adds infrastructure and a new failure mode (missed chunks). Fine-tuning (B) is a poor way to supply factual knowledge. One agent per policy (D) fragments exactly the cross-document reasoning that is needed.

questions.stem: A requirement says data must be processed only within the client's AWS account boundary. A developer proposes using the Claude Platform on AWS because it is purchased through AWS Marketplace and supports features earlier. What should you check first?
options: Only whether the Claude Platform on AWS offers the latest model versions the team wants to use.
Which party processes the data: the Claude Platform on AWS calls Anthropic's API, unlike Bedrock.
Whether the Claude Platform on AWS supports PrivateLink, since private connectivity means data stays in the account.
Nothing further: purchasing through AWS Marketplace means processing happens inside the client's AWS account.
questions.explanation: Procurement route, network path and data processor are different things. Anthropic's documentation describes the two AWS offerings as differing in architecture, API surface and feature availability. Governance constraints filter options before features do, so clarify the requirement and match it to the right offering. Assuming Marketplace equals in-boundary processing (D) is the trap, and private connectivity (C) controls the network path, not which party processes the data.

questions.stem: An HR inbox classifier routes messages into 6 categories. On a test set of 2,000 messages, accuracy is 94%. The 'harassment report' class makes up 2% of messages. The client's priority is that harassment reports are never missed. Which metric should be the primary acceptance criterion?
options: Weighted F1 across all six classes, since it combines precision and recall and accounts for class imbalance.
The model's average self-reported confidence on harassment reports, with a target above 0.9.
Overall accuracy of at least 95% on a test set stratified by month, which captures all categories including harassment reports.
Recall for the harassment-report class (with its precision monitored), reported alongside per-class precision, recall and F1.
questions.explanation: For a rare, high-stakes class, overall accuracy and weighted F1 are dominated by common classes; a classifier could miss every harassment report and still score 94% or more. The business requirement ('never miss') maps to recall for that class, with precision watched to keep reviewer load manageable. Confidence (B) is not a measure of correctness.

questions.stem: Two prompt versions for a 12-label classifier are compared. Version B has higher weighted F1 (0.91 vs. 0.90) but lower macro F1 (0.79 vs. 0.86). Rare labels drive regulatory reporting. Which version should ship, and why?
options: Version B, because weighted F1 is the standard headline metric for multi-class classifiers and B is higher.
Version B, because weighted F1 reflects the real traffic mix and therefore the experience of most users.
Neither can be chosen from F1; compare overall accuracy, which is the appropriate metric for multi-class tasks.
Version A: macro F1 weights every label equally, so B's drop signals regressions on the rare, critical labels.
questions.explanation: Weighted F1 can rise while rare classes get worse, because common classes dominate the weighting. Macro F1 exposes rare-class regressions. Since rare labels matter most here, A is safer, subject to checking per-class numbers. Accuracy (C) has the same blind spot as weighted F1.

questions.stem: A grading system outputs exactly one of 12 rubric labels for each essay. You have 1,200 essays labeled by expert graders. How should the system's correctness be graded?
options: Code-based exact match, summarized as a confusion matrix with per-class metrics and ordinal metrics.
An LLM judge that scores each output's quality from 1 to 10 against the rubric, averaged across the 1,200 essays.
Compare the system's written justifications with the experts' using semantic similarity of embeddings.
Expert re-review of a random 5% sample of outputs, which is how the original labels were produced.
questions.explanation: When the output is a discrete label with a known correct answer, grade it deterministically in code; it is cheap, reproducible and objective. Ordinal metrics capture 'how wrong' for ordered grades. An LLM judge (B) adds cost and its own errors to a problem code solves exactly. A small sample (D) cannot measure per-class performance across 12 labels. Similarity of justifications (C) does not measure whether the label is correct.

questions.stem: You plan to use Claude as a pairwise judge to compare two summarization prompts on 500 articles. Which TWO practices most improve the judge's reliability?
options: Calibrate the judge against human ratings on a sample and refine the rubric until they agree.
Tell the judge which output came from the new prompt and what it was designed to improve, so it evaluates the right aspects.
Instruct the judge to prefer the more complete summary when quality is otherwise similar, which rewards coverage.
Ask a single 'Which is better?' question without a rubric, so the judge applies its own holistic judgment.
Run each comparison twice with positions swapped and count only consistent verdicts (or treat inconsistent ones as ties).
questions.explanation: LLM judges have systematic biases (position, verbosity, self-preference) and must be validated against humans. Calibration establishes trust, and order-swapping neutralizes position bias. Revealing which is the new prompt (B) biases the verdict. Favoring length (C) is a known bias. A rubric-free question (D) increases inconsistency.

questions.stem: A vendor announces a new model that is 'better on every benchmark.' Your production assistant uses a pinned older model. What is the correct gate before switching?
options: Switch after reviewing the vendor's published benchmarks across reasoning, coding and safety, since they are broader than an internal suite.
Run your own regression suite on the candidate model, then roll it out gradually while monitoring.
Have the new model review a sample of the old model's outputs and report whether it would have answered better.
Switch for one week on all traffic and roll back if complaint volume rises above the previous week's level.
questions.explanation: Evaluations are the required gate before a model swap. Public benchmarks do not measure your prompts, formats, edge cases or cost profile. Gradual rollout catches what offline evaluation misses. Using customer complaints as the test (D) exposes users to regressions. Self-assessment (C) is meaningless.

questions.stem: You want production evidence for a new prompt on a high-stakes claims workflow before any customer sees its outputs. Which approach provides that?
options: Shadow testing: run real inputs through the new prompt in parallel, off the customer path.
An A/B test with a small share of customers on the new prompt, monitored closely so problems are caught quickly.
Offline evaluation on a large synthetic dataset generated to match production claim types.
A canary release to 5% of customers with automatic rollback if error rates exceed the current baseline.
questions.explanation: Shadow mode gives real input distributions with no customer exposure, which suits high-stakes changes before any A/B or canary step. A/B tests and canaries (B, D) expose real customers. Synthetic data alone (C) misses the real distribution.

questions.stem: You A/B test two versions of a conversational support assistant, with resolution rate as the primary metric. The initial design randomizes assignment per request. Why is that a problem, and what should you do?
options: It is fine; per-request randomization maximizes the number of samples and gives the fastest statistically valid result.
Randomize per day instead, alternating variants each day, which keeps every conversation on a single variant.
Run the test only on weekends, when traffic is lower and more homogeneous, to reduce noise in the comparison.
Randomize per user or conversation so each conversation stays on one variant, and fix the metric and sample size in advance.
questions.explanation: The unit of randomization must match the unit of outcome; conversational resolution is per conversation or user. Pre-registering the metric and sample size, and not stopping early on a promising result, avoids false positives. Alternating by day (B) confounds the variant with day-of-week effects. Weekend-only testing (C) is unrepresentative.

questions.stem: A RAG assistant states a policy detail that is not in the knowledge base. To decide whether this is a retrieval problem or a generation problem, what should you check first?
options: Whether the relevant source passage was present in the retrieved context for that query, which tells you which stage failed.
Whether the answer was longer than the median response, since longer answers are more prone to invention.
Whether users rated the answer positively, since a liked answer suggests the detail may be acceptable.
Whether the generator's temperature is high enough to cause invented details, and lower it if so.
questions.explanation: Separate the pipeline stages. Inspecting what was actually retrieved tells you which stage failed and therefore which fix applies. Temperature (D) is a guess. User satisfaction (C) and length (B) do not locate the fault.

questions.stem: A team moved its whole contract-analysis pipeline to a smaller, faster model to save cost. Clause classification accuracy is unchanged, but multi-step questions ('Does the termination clause interact with the auto-renewal clause to create a gap?') now fail 3x more often. What is the most accurate diagnosis and fix?
options: Hallucination: the smaller model invents clause interactions, which an explicit 'do not speculate' instruction will fix.
Retrieval failure: multi-step questions need more clauses, so raise top-k for those questions.
A prompt failure: the prompts were written for the larger model and need rewriting for the smaller one across the board.
Model mismatch; route multi-step reasoning to a more capable model and keep the small one for classification.
questions.explanation: The failure pattern (fine on simple tasks, worse on complex reasoning after a model change) points to a capability mismatch, not to prompts or retrieval. Routing by task complexity keeps most of the savings and restores quality. The other diagnoses do not match the evidence.

questions.stem: After a prompt edit meant to improve tone, overall accuracy of a 9-class router drops from 92% to 90%. What is the most efficient next diagnostic step?
options: Revert immediately, since any regression in a production router is unacceptable and tone is a secondary concern.
Compare per-class metrics and confusion matrices for both versions on the same test set.
Grow the test set until the two versions' accuracy converges, to confirm whether the drop is real.
Run the new prompt at several temperatures to check whether the drop is caused by sampling variability.
questions.explanation: A two-point aggregate drop could be one class collapsing or noise spread across all classes. A per-class comparison localizes the regression and shows which instruction caused it. Reverting (A) loses the tone improvement without understanding the cause. Adding data to make the difference disappear (C) is not diagnosis. Temperature (D) is unrelated.

questions.stem: You are building an evaluation dataset for an insurance claims assistant. Which THREE properties matter most?
options: It includes edge cases, known failure modes and adversarial inputs.
It reflects the real production mix of claim types and channels.
It grows only with cases confirmed as correct in production, so its labels are known to be reliable.
It is generated by the model under test from claim templates, giving large volume and full coverage of categories.
It has expert-verified expected outcomes, with enough examples per category to measure per-category performance.
questions.explanation: A good evaluation set is representative, stress-tests known risks and has trustworthy labels with enough coverage per segment. Having the evaluated model write the test set (D) bakes in its own blind spots. Adding only passing cases (C) produces inflated scores and hides regressions.

questions.stem: A grant-scoring assistant outputs an ordinal score from 1 to 10. Version X has 41% exact-match accuracy and 88% of its scores within one point of the expert's. Version Y has 47% exact match but only 74% within one point, with occasional misses of 4 to 6 points. Funding decisions use thresholds at 6 and 8. Which version is better for this use, and why?
options: Y, because exact-match accuracy is the most direct measure of agreement with the experts and Y is 6 points higher.
Neither can be chosen without an LLM judge to assess the quality of each score's justification.
Y, because its large misses are rare outliers and exact agreement is what reviewers will notice.
X, because for ordinal scores error size matters, and Y's large misses can flip funding decisions across the 6 and 8 thresholds.
questions.explanation: Exact match treats an off-by-one score the same as a 6-point miss. With decision thresholds, big misses are the costly errors. Ordinal-aware metrics and decision-level agreement reflect the real impact. Rare but large errors (C) are exactly what flips outcomes.

questions.stem: An essay-feedback tool gives the same essay a B on one run and a C+ on the next, with temperature already at 0. Accuracy on the test set looks acceptable. Which evaluation is missing, and what improvements typically help?
options: Nothing is missing: accuracy on the test set is acceptable, so run-to-run differences average out across users.
A larger test set, since more items will give a more stable accuracy estimate and reveal the problem.
A consistency check across repeated runs, improved with anchored rubrics and per-criterion reasoning.
A latency evaluation, since inconsistent grades often come from timeouts that truncate the model's reasoning.
questions.explanation: Run-to-run variation is invisible in a single-pass accuracy number, but users experience it as unfairness. Repeated-run measurement exposes it, and anchored rubrics and criterion-by-criterion reasoning reduce it. Latency (D) and test-set size (B) do not measure consistency.

questions.stem: Two agent designs are compared for invoice dispute resolution. Design A costs $0.04 per request with a 52% resolution rate. Design B costs $0.09 per request with an 81% resolution rate. Unresolved disputes go to humans at $6 each. Which metric should drive the choice?
options: Total cost per resolved dispute, including the cost of human handling for disputes the AI does not resolve.
Cost per request, since it is the cost the team directly controls and A is less than half the price of B.
Tokens per request, since token volume drives the API bill and is the most precise measure of efficiency.
Resolution rate alone, since a higher resolution rate always means lower total cost.
questions.explanation: Per-request token cost ignores downstream costs. Per 100 requests: A costs $4 plus 48 escalations at $6 ($288), about $292; B costs $9 plus 19 escalations ($114), about $123. Evaluation should use business-level unit economics, not proxy metrics like cost per request (B) or tokens (C). Resolution rate alone (D) ignores what each resolution costs; it happens to favor B here but would mislead if B were far more expensive.

questions.stem: A streaming chat assistant reports an average latency of 1.1 s. Users still complain it feels slow. Which TWO latency metrics should the team track instead of, or in addition to, the average?
options: Time to first token, which drives perceived responsiveness in streaming interfaces.
Tail latency percentiles (p95, p99) of end-to-end response time.
Median output length, since longer outputs take longer to stream and feel slower.
Aggregate tokens per second across all users, which captures overall system throughput.
Total API calls per day, to detect load spikes that might slow the service.
questions.explanation: Averages hide the slow tail that frustrated users experience, and in streaming interfaces the wait before the first token is what feels slow. Output length (C) and request counts (E) are not latency. Aggregate throughput (D) also hides the per-request tail.

questions.stem: Before launching a public-facing benefits assistant, the team needs to evaluate safety. Which TWO evaluation components are most important?
options: A load test at peak traffic, confirming that safety classifiers keep their latency under the SLA.
A red-team set of adversarial prompts, measured as attack success rate.
An over-refusal set of legitimate sensitive questions, measured as false-refusal rate.
A review of the system prompt's safety instructions by the legal team, signed off before launch.
A count of apologies and disclaimers in responses, as a signal of cautious behavior.
questions.explanation: Safety evaluation must measure both directions: whether harmful requests succeed, and whether legitimate sensitive requests are wrongly refused. A system tuned only against attacks often over-refuses and fails users. The other options do not measure safety.

questions.stem: After a release, input token cost rises 4x with no traffic change. Responses show cache_read_input_tokens near zero, whereas last week it was about 85% of input tokens. What is the most likely cause, and how should it be monitored?
options: The provider changed its pricing, so the cost increase is external and the response is a budget adjustment.
Users started asking longer questions after the release, increasing the uncached part of each request.
The cache TTL was switched to 1 hour by the release, raising write costs on every request.
The release changed content before the breakpoint; monitor cache hit rate and alert on drops.
questions.explanation: A sudden collapse in cache reads with no traffic change points to a prefix that is no longer stable. Cache hit rate is a key cost-optimization metric and should be monitored with alerts. Longer questions (B) would not remove cache reads. TTLs (C) do not change by themselves.

questions.stem: An employee-help assistant performed well for months. After the company launched a new benefits program, the 'not found in documents' rate rose from 4% to 19% and escalations doubled, while retrieval latency and errors are unchanged. What is happening, and what should monitoring have included?
options: Input drift into topics the index lacks; monitor not-found and escalation rates by topic.
A partial retrieval outage is returning empty results for some queries.
Normal seasonal variation; wait a few weeks to see whether rates return to baseline.
The model's quality has degraded over time, so it should be replaced with a newer version.
questions.explanation: A topic shift after a business event, with healthy infrastructure, indicates distribution drift and a content gap. Behavioral metrics (not-found rate, escalations, clusters of unanswered topics) catch it, and the fix is to ingest the new content and extend the evaluation set. Pinned models do not degrade on their own (D). There is no outage signal (B). Waiting (C) wastes time.

questions.stem: A RAG team only tracks final answer correctness. Answer quality dropped after a chunking change, and the team cannot tell why. Which additional metric family would have made the cause obvious?
options: Average answer length before and after, since shorter answers indicate missing context.
Retrieval metrics such as recall@k and MRR, tracked separately from answer quality.
The number of chunks in the index before and after the change, since more chunks dilutes retrieval.
Average generator latency, since slower generation indicates the model is struggling with the context.
questions.explanation: Measuring retrieval on its own (did the right passage appear, and how high) separates retrieval regressions from generation regressions. A chunking change mainly affects retrieval, so recall@k would have shown the drop directly. Index size (C), answer length (A) and generator latency (D) do not measure whether the right passages were retrieved.

questions.stem: An auditor asks how you verify that the policy assistant's answers are faithful to the source documents. Which approach is most defensible at scale?
options: Ask an LLM judge to rate each answer's overall faithfulness from 1 to 10 and report the average.
Rely on the system prompt instruction to use only the provided documents, which the model follows reliably.
Citations, programmatic checks of cited text, a calibrated judge, and human audit of samples.
Have the policy team review ten answers per quarter and attest to their accuracy.
questions.explanation: Faithfulness at scale needs layers: citations make claims traceable (and the feature only returns pointers to provided documents), code checks the mechanics, a calibrated judge assesses whether claims are supported, and humans audit samples. Trusting instructions (B), an uncalibrated overall score (A) or tiny samples (D) do not hold up to an audit.

questions.stem: A team changes the system prompt, the retrieval top-k, the reranker and the model in one release. Quality improves 6 points overall but one critical category regresses 9 points. What process failure does this reveal?
options: Bundling several changes without per-change evaluation, so the regression can't be attributed.
Releasing without a code freeze, so last-minute changes slipped in without review.
Using too small a reranker, which interacts badly with the new model on that category.
Evaluating with exact-match metrics instead of an LLM judge, which would have caught the regression.
questions.explanation: Iterative improvement requires attributable changes: with versioned prompts, configurations and models, each evaluated against the same fixed set, you know which change caused which effect. Bundled changes make regressions impossible to diagnose. The other options do not address attribution.

questions.stem: An extraction prompt scores 98% on the evaluation set. Investigation shows that the five few-shot examples in the prompt were copied from that evaluation set. What is the problem, and how should it be fixed?
options: The model is overfitting to the examples; lower the temperature to reduce reliance on them.
Test leakage; draw examples from a separate dev pool and re-score on held-out data.
No problem: few-shot examples should come from real labeled data, and the evaluation set is the best labeled data available.
Remove all few-shot examples so the prompt cannot overlap with the evaluation set.
questions.explanation: Evaluation data must be held out from anything used to build the prompt, or scores overstate real performance. Few-shot examples should come from a separate development pool. Real data is fine as long as it is not the test set (C). Removing useful examples entirely (D) throws away a legitimate technique.

questions.stem: A hospital network has signed Anthropic's BAA and enabled a HIPAA-ready API organization. The CIO says, 'We're covered, so the app is HIPAA compliant.' Which TWO statements correct this view?
options: Coverage is feature-specific, and data sent to third-party services sits outside the BAA.
The hospital must still meet HIPAA itself: access controls, audit logs, minimum-necessary use, and protection of PHI in its logs, caches and indexes.
The BAA extends to every Anthropic product the hospital's staff use, including individual plans, as long as they use work email addresses.
With a BAA in place, PHI can be included in any prompt or feature, since Anthropic is now contractually responsible for protecting it.
HIPAA applies to the hospital's records systems, not to AI processing services, so the BAA is a formality.
questions.explanation: Being HIPAA-eligible (the vendor will sign a BAA for specific services) is different from being compliant (your whole implementation meets the rules). Coverage is feature-specific, and the customer remains responsible for its own safeguards. Consumer plans cannot enable HIPAA coverage (C). PHI use still follows minimum-necessary rules (D). HIPAA applies regardless of technology (E).

questions.stem: An EU customer exercises the GDPR right to erasure against a support platform built on Claude. Which THREE locations must the erasure process cover?
options: Public help-center articles that were used as retrieval sources in the customer's conversations.
Logs, transcripts and cached responses that contain the customer's data.
The foundation model's weights, which must be retrained without the customer's data.
Evaluation and test datasets that were built from production conversations including the customer.
Chunks and embeddings in the vector index derived from the customer's tickets and emails, including archived copies.
questions.explanation: Personal data spreads into derived stores: vector indexes, logs, caches, transcripts and evaluation sets. Erasure processes must cover them, which is why chunks should carry source and subject identifiers. Using a pretrained model through an API does not put your customer's data into its weights (C). Pages that never held the data (A) are out of scope. Also confirm the provider's retention terms for API data.

questions.stem: A claims-triage feature sends full customer records (name, address, SSN, medical history and 40 other fields) to Claude, although the task only needs the incident description, policy type and claim amount. Which principle is violated, and what is the fix?
options: Fairness: remove the address and zip code fields, which can act as proxies for protected characteristics.
Transparency: add a notice to outputs stating which customer data was used to produce each triage decision.
Data minimization (minimum necessary): send only the fields the task needs and pseudonymize any required identifiers.
No principle is violated; the extra context improves accuracy and all fields are already in the insurer's own systems.
questions.explanation: GDPR's data minimization principle and HIPAA's minimum-necessary standard both require limiting personal data to what the purpose needs. Pseudonymization keeps references usable while reducing exposure. A disclaimer (B) does not reduce exposure. Removing one field (A) is incomplete. Extra fields add risk and can distract the model (D).

questions.stem: A federal agency program office wants a Claude-based document assistant. Its authorization to operate (ATO) covers workloads only within specific, FedRAMP-authorized cloud environments. What should drive the architecture first?
options: Procurement simplicity: start with individual subscriptions for the program office while the formal authorization process runs.
Governance constraints first: design only within Claude options authorized for the agency's environment.
Model capability: choose the highest-scoring model on public benchmarks, then work with the agency to extend the ATO to cover its hosting.
Speed to value: prototype on the public API with representative agency documents, then migrate to an authorized environment for production.
questions.explanation: Compliance requirements filter the option space before performance and cost trade-offs. An offering outside the authorized boundary is not an option, however capable it is. Benchmark-first selection (C), prototyping on unauthorized services with real data (D) and individual subscriptions outside a governed deployment (A) all risk violating the ATO.

questions.stem: A lender uses Claude to draft adverse-action rationale for declined small-business loans. Regulators require that declines be explainable and reviewed. What human-in-the-loop design is most appropriate?
options: Human review of a random 10% of declines, with the review rate increased if the error rate exceeds a threshold.
Human review whenever an applicant disputes a decline, with automatic reversal if the reviewer disagrees.
Claude drafts cited rationales; a credit officer approves every decline; overrides are logged.
Automated declines with the rationale emailed to applicants, plus a monthly compliance review of a risk-based sample.
questions.explanation: High-impact decisions affecting individuals call for mandatory human review, with grounded drafts that make review efficient and auditable, and logged overrides that improve the system. Full automation (D) and sampled or complaint-driven review (A, B) leave most adverse decisions without the required oversight.

questions.stem: A refund agent's system prompt says 'Never issue refunds above $500 without manager approval.' During testing, a user persuades the agent that 'the manager already approved it in another chat,' and a $900 refund goes through. What is the correct control?
options: Enforce the limit in the refund tool's code using the order's value from the system of record, routing $500 or more to an approval queue.
Add a verifier agent that reviews each refund decision against the policy before the tool is called.
Set temperature to 0 so the agent applies the policy deterministically and is less susceptible to persuasion.
Strengthen the prompt: state the limit in several places, add examples of manipulation attempts, and require the agent to quote the policy before refunding.
questions.explanation: Hard business rules belong in deterministic code at the point of action, using trusted data rather than model-supplied amounts or claims. Prompts guide behavior; they do not enforce it. Louder prompts (D), agent-on-agent checks (B) and temperature (C) are all still probabilistic.

questions.stem: An executive-assistant agent reads incoming email and can send email, schedule meetings and share documents. Security is concerned about prompt injection through inbound messages. Which TWO controls most reduce the risk of harmful actions?
options: Scope credentials and tools to the minimum needed, such as internal-only sharing.
Have the model classify each email as trustworthy or not, and follow embedded requests only from trustworthy senders.
Add a detailed catalog of known injection techniques to the system prompt so the model recognizes them.
Require explicit user confirmation for outbound or irreversible actions, showing the exact action before it runs.
Turn off logging of email content, so injected instructions are not retained or replayed.
questions.explanation: Assume some injections will succeed and limit the damage: human confirmation for consequential actions and least-privilege capabilities. Model-based trust classification (B) can itself be manipulated. Long lists of known attacks (C) miss new ones. Disabling logging (E) removes detection and audit.

questions.stem: A recruiting team wants Claude to shortlist applicants. They propose removing name, gender and age fields from résumés to make it fair. Which TWO points should you raise?
options: Removing protected attributes does not ensure fairness, because proxies such as schools, graduation years or zip codes correlate with protected groups.
Higher temperature reduces systematic bias by introducing randomness into which candidates are shortlisted.
Shortlisting is advisory and humans make the final hire, so fairness obligations apply only at the hiring decision.
With protected fields removed, the model cannot discriminate, so a one-time check at launch is sufficient.
Measure outcomes: compare shortlisting rates across groups on a representative test set and in production, with humans accountable.
questions.explanation: Blinding inputs is insufficient because of proxy variables. Fairness has to be measured on outcomes and governed with human accountability. Shortlisting is a consequential decision that shapes who is considered (C). Randomness (B) is not fairness. Skipping evaluation (D) leaves bias undetected.

questions.stem: A public benefits portal will deploy a Claude assistant to help residents understand eligibility. Which transparency practice is most important?
options: Keep answers short by omitting sources, since residents mainly want a quick yes or no on eligibility.
Disclose AI involvement in the portal's terms of service, which residents accept when creating an account.
Disclose clearly that residents are using AI, show the policy sources behind answers and the assistant's limits, and offer a path to a caseworker.
Give the assistant a friendly human name and persona so residents feel comfortable, while noting AI use in the privacy policy.
questions.explanation: Transparency means people know they are dealing with AI, can see where answers come from, understand what the system can and cannot do, and can reach a human. Impersonating a human (D) is deceptive. Hiding sources (A) or burying the disclosure (B) undermines informed use.

questions.stem: An internal legal-research assistant sometimes returns plausible but nonexistent case citations. Lawyers have nearly filed one. Which mitigation directly targets this failure mode?
options: Limit answers to a short summary without citations, so there are no citations to fabricate.
Ground answers in a verified corpus with citations, validate them, and require attorney sign-off.
Use a lower temperature and a more capable model, which together sharply reduce fabricated citations.
Strengthen the system prompt to require citing only real cases with full reporter citations, and to say when unsure.
questions.explanation: Fabricated citations are a known failure mode. Grounding in provided documents, structured citations that point only to supplied sources, programmatic checks and human verification together address it. Prompt instructions (D) and model or temperature changes (C) reduce but do not prevent fabrication. Dropping citations (A) removes the lawyers' means of verification.

questions.stem: A consumer chat app streams Claude's answers word by word for responsiveness. A policy classifier runs in parallel on the user's input, but harmful content occasionally reaches the screen before the classifier flags the request. What is the correct design?
options: Run the classifier on the complete answer after it is displayed, and retract the message if it is flagged.
Buffer streamed output until the fast classifier passes, and add output screening.
Turn off streaming and return answers only after the input classifier has finished, accepting the added latency.
Add a report button, so users can flag harmful content for removal and review.
questions.explanation: Parallel guardrails save latency only if the release of output is gated on their verdict. Output screening catches harmful answers to innocuous-looking requests. Dropping streaming (C) gives up responsiveness unnecessarily. Post-display checks (A) and user reports (D) come too late.

questions.stem: To reduce cost, a team caches final answers keyed by normalized question text. Executives and staff use the same assistant, and some answers draw on executive-only compensation documents. What is the risk, and what is the fix?
options: Encrypt the cache at rest and in transit, so cached executive answers are protected.
Answers built from restricted documents can be served to unauthorized users; include the permission scope in the cache key.
Shorten cache expiry to one minute, so a restricted answer is unlikely to be requested by someone else in that window.
No risk: the cache stores only final answers, not the restricted source documents themselves.
questions.explanation: An answer derived from restricted data is itself restricted. Caches must respect authorization boundaries and be invalidated when content or permissions change. A short TTL (C) narrows the window but does not close it. Encryption (A) protects data at rest but does not stop it being served to the wrong user.

questions.stem: A security team wants to prevent Claude Code from reading .env files and secrets across all developer machines in the organization. Which TWO controls provide the strongest enforcement?
options: Developer training on not pasting secrets into prompts, with a signed acknowledgment.
Enable sandboxing through managed settings, with OS-level filesystem read restrictions on secret paths.
A line in each repository's CLAUDE.md telling Claude not to read .env files or secrets.
A deny rule for .env in each developer's user settings, set up during onboarding.
Managed deny rules for secret paths, with bypass mode disabled.
questions.explanation: Managed deny rules are the organization-wide permission layer and take precedence over user and project settings. Disabling bypass mode prevents a developer from turning off all checks. Because permission rules act on Claude Code's tools and recognized commands, while a script could still open a file, OS-level sandboxing closes the remaining gap. CLAUDE.md (C) is guidance, not enforcement. User settings (D) can be changed by the user. Training (A) is not a technical control.

questions.stem: A public-facing assistant is being targeted by users trying to jailbreak it into producing prohibited content and to extract its system prompt. Which TWO measures form the strongest layered defense?
options: Screen inputs and outputs with classifiers, gating what is displayed, and log flagged attempts.
Rely on the model's built-in safety training, which is designed to resist jailbreaks and prompt extraction.
Put a confidential instruction in the system prompt that the model must never reveal its prompt or discuss its rules.
Raise the temperature so responses vary and attackers cannot iterate toward a working jailbreak.
Application-layer abuse controls: rate limits, per-account anomaly monitoring, and blocking of repeat offenders.
questions.explanation: Effective defenses combine content-level screening with platform-level abuse controls. Built-in model safety is a valuable layer but not the only one (B). Secrets in prompts (C) are a target, not a defense. Temperature (D) does not improve safety.

questions.stem: An HR assistant drafts responses to employee relations cases, some involving discipline and termination recommendations. Leadership wants to auto-send drafts to save time. What is the appropriate governance decision?
options: Do not use AI for employee relations at all, because any error carries legal risk.
Auto-send all drafts with an 'AI-generated' label so employees know to verify the content.
Auto-send all drafts, since testing showed high accuracy and HR can correct any issue afterwards.
Tier by impact: automate low-risk answers; require HR approval for discipline and termination.
questions.explanation: Human oversight should scale with impact. Decisions with significant effects on individuals need review and accountability, while low-risk content can be automated with monitoring. All-or-nothing approaches (A, C) either over-automate or forgo safe value. A label (B) does not provide oversight.

questions.stem: An EU insurer requires that personal data be processed in the EU. The team deploys Claude through Amazon Bedrock and selects the global endpoint for best availability. What is the issue?
options: A global endpoint may route across regions; use in-region inference in the EU instead.
Nothing: Bedrock processes requests in the region where the API is called, regardless of endpoint type.
Use the global endpoint but encrypt requests, which keeps the data under EU jurisdiction.
Residency rules cover where data is stored, not where it is processed, so the endpoint choice does not matter.
questions.explanation: Endpoint choice affects where inference runs. Bedrock offers both global (cross-region routing) and in-region options, and residency rules usually concern processing, not only storage (D). Bedrock does not always process in the calling region (B). Encryption (C) protects data in transit but does not change where it is processed.

questions.stem: A team plans to use Claude to summarize employee performance reviews. A privacy officer asks what failure modes and limitations must be documented before approval. Which response is most complete?
options: 'We will monitor employee complaints after launch and address issues as they arise.'
'Testing showed high accuracy, so there are no material limitations to document beyond normal software risk.'
Document each known failure mode, the control that mitigates it, the residual risk, and the escalation path.
'Model errors are covered by the vendor's terms, so liability for limitations rests with the vendor.'
questions.explanation: Governance requires an honest inventory of risks with a mitigating control for each and acknowledged residual risk. Claims of no limitations (B), purely reactive monitoring (A) and shifting responsibility to the vendor (D) do not meet that standard.

questions.stem: A shared Claude Code configuration allows developers to run the agent in bypass-permissions mode for speed. A security review flags that this turns off all permission checks. What organizational control addresses this?
options: Uninstall Claude Code from developer machines until a safer configuration is available.
Publish a policy asking developers not to use bypass mode, and review compliance quarterly.
Reset each developer's local settings file weekly through a scheduled script.
Disable bypass mode in managed settings and use managed allow rules for speed.
questions.explanation: Managed settings are the enforcement layer that users cannot override, and Claude Code's documentation provides a specific setting to disable bypass mode. Speed can be preserved with deliberate allow rules rather than disabling all checks. Requests (B) are not controls. Removal (A) and deleting files (C) are blunt or easily circumvented.

questions.stem: An agent will be allowed to modify production data (closing tickets, updating CRM fields, issuing credits). Which TWO risk controls are most important to design in from the start?
options: A reversible audit trail of every action, with model and prompt versions.
Have the model assess each action's risk and request approval when it judges an action risky.
Broad database credentials matching the DBA team, so the agent never fails for lack of permissions.
Unlimited automatic retries on failed writes, so transient errors never leave work incomplete.
Tiered autonomy: low-impact reversible actions run automatically, while high-impact actions need human approval enforced in code.
questions.explanation: Autonomy should match risk and be enforced deterministically, and every action should be auditable and reversible. Unlimited retries (D) risk duplicate side effects. Broad credentials (C) violate least privilege. Model self-judgment (B) is not an enforcement mechanism.

questions.stem: A clinic wants to summarize visit notes with Claude while minimizing PHI exposure, and asks whether de-identifying the notes first means HIPAA no longer applies to the pipeline. What is the most accurate answer?
options: Yes: removing patient names and medical record numbers is enough to de-identify clinical notes.
Only if it meets Safe Harbor or Expert Determination; free text often hides identifiers.
No: HIPAA applies to all medical text, even when fully de-identified, so de-identification has no effect.
Yes, as long as the model is instructed not to retain or repeat any personal information.
questions.explanation: Properly de-identified data is not PHI, but the bar is specific, and clinical free text routinely contains identifiers beyond names (dates, locations, relatives, record numbers). Removing names alone (A) does not meet the standard. De-identified data is not restricted by the Privacy Rule (C). Instructions to the model (D) are irrelevant to the legal status of the data.

questions.stem: In a kickoff meeting, a client's VP says the contract must guarantee '100% accurate answers' from the Claude-based policy assistant. How should you respond?
options: Agree to the requirement in principle, and define 'accurate' narrowly in the statement of work so it can be met with prompt tuning.
Explain that no AI or human process is 100% accurate, and propose a measured target on an agreed eval set, plus safeguards and monitoring.
Counter-propose 99.9% accuracy, which is achievable with a strong model and shows commitment to quality.
Decline the requirement and the engagement, since accepting an impossible guarantee would create contractual liability.
questions.explanation: Setting realistic expectations early prevents later disputes. A measured target on an agreed test set, plus layered safeguards, is honest and verifiable. Agreeing to 100% (A) or picking an arbitrary near-perfect figure (C) creates commitments you cannot meet or prove. Refusing (D) abandons a solvable expectation problem.

questions.stem: You are running structured discovery for a proposed contract-review assistant. Which THREE pieces of information most change the architecture and should be gathered before any design work?
options: Who acts on the output and how: the reviewer workflow, approvals, latency expectations and integration points.
The full list of contract types the client might want to support in the next three years.
The current baseline (time, error rate, cost per contract) and the success metric the sponsor will judge by.
The client's preferred model vendor and version, so the design can be optimized for it from the start.
Data types, volume, sensitivity, residency and approved vendor routes.
questions.explanation: Baselines and success metrics define value; data and compliance constraints filter feasible options; the consuming workflow shapes the output, latency and human-in-the-loop design. A vendor preference (D) is a late, secondary input that must pass your own constraints and evaluations. A three-year wish list (B) is scope for later phases, not what shapes the first architecture.

questions.stem: A client insists on a 5-agent architecture for an HR FAQ assistant because 'multi-agent is the modern approach.' Your analysis suggests a single model with retrieval and two tools would suffice. What is the best way to handle this?
options: Build the 5-agent architecture as specified, since the client owns the requirements and has experience with the approach.
Build the single-model design and present it as a streamlined multi-agent system, since the client cares about the outcome.
Escalate to the client's executive sponsor to override the technical team's preference.
Ask what each agent uniquely needs, compare costs with a simpler design, and add agents only on evidence.
questions.explanation: Architects defend designs by naming costs and credible alternatives, and they ground decisions in what each component must uniquely do. Evidence-gated incrementalism respects the client's goal while avoiding unjustified complexity. Silent substitution (B) breaks trust. Escalation (C) is premature.

questions.stem: You need approval for a design that uses prompt caching and a tiered-model router. Your audience is the CFO, who is not technical. Which explanation is most effective?
options: Translate it into business terms: projected cost per resolution, quality checks and the main risk.
Show a detailed table of token counts and prices per call for both designs, so the CFO can verify the arithmetic.
Walk through how caching stores computed state for the prompt prefix and how routing uses a classifier, so the CFO understands why it works.
Note that both techniques are documented best practices from the vendor, so they are low-risk by definition.
questions.explanation: Communicating trade-offs means translating them into the audience's terms: cost, risk and outcomes, with the evidence and the monitoring plan. Mechanism detail (B, C) fits engineers, not a CFO. An appeal to authority (D) gives no basis for a decision.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, a new engineering lead asks why the system uses full-context inclusion instead of RAG, and whether to switch. Nobody remembers the reasoning. Which practice would have prevented this?
options: Architecture decision records, including alternatives and triggers for revisiting.
A system overview page listing each component and technology in the architecture.
Recordings of all design meetings stored in the team's shared drive.
Detailed code comments in the retrieval and prompt-assembly modules explaining what the code does.
questions.explanation: ADRs preserve the why, including alternatives and the triggers for revisiting, which is exactly what a successor needs. Comments (D) describe code, not architecture. Meeting recordings (C) are unsearchable in practice. A technology list (B) omits the reasoning.

questions.stem: Your team is handing a production Claude application over to the client's operations team. Which THREE handoff artifacts are most important for them to run and evolve the system safely?
options: Runbooks and dashboards: what to monitor, alert thresholds, and incident and escalation procedures.
Versioned prompts and configuration with change history.
The evaluation suite and how to run it before any change.
The full project plan and status reports, so the operations team understands how the system was built.
Recordings of the user-training sessions run during launch.
questions.explanation: Operating and changing an LLM system safely requires the means to test changes (evaluations), the current state and history (versioned configuration) and the means to detect and respond to problems (monitoring and runbooks). Project plans (D) and training recordings (E) do not help the client operate or change the system.

questions.stem: A client wants a contractual SLA of 'responses in under 1 second.' Measurements show a median of 0.8 s and a p95 of 2.7 s for full answers, with time to first token at a p95 of 0.6 s when streaming. What SLA should you propose?
options: Accept the 1-second SLA measured as average full-response time, since the median is already 0.8 seconds.
Propose SLAs on p95 time to first token and p95 completion time, with a defined measurement method and exclusions.
Commit to a p99 of 1 second and plan an optimization sprint to reach it after launch.
Decline to commit to latency SLAs, since LLM response times depend on output length and cannot be guaranteed.
questions.explanation: Align SLA expectations with how the system actually behaves and how users perceive it. Percentile-based and first-token metrics, with defined measurement, are realistic and verifiable. Averages (A) hide the tail. Refusing an SLA (D) is unhelpful. Committing to a target the data shows you will miss (C) is setting up a breach.

questions.stem: A large insurer wants Claude in 14 business processes at once. Budget and stakeholder patience are limited. What lifecycle approach do you recommend?
options: Let each business unit choose its own use case and vendor, so ownership stays with the people closest to the work.
Build a general-purpose AI platform for a year first, so all 14 processes can launch on a solid, consistent foundation.
Start with one or two high-volume, low-risk processes, prove results, then expand.
Launch all 14 in parallel with a shared platform team, so momentum builds and lessons are learned quickly across processes.
questions.explanation: A focused pilot with clear metrics produces evidence and reusable foundations, building stakeholder confidence for later phases. A big-bang launch (D) spreads effort and multiplies risk. A platform-first approach with no use cases (B) delays value. Fragmented vendors (A) lose shared governance.

questions.stem: Halfway through design, the client's legal team says, 'No customer data may leave our cloud account,' which rules out your planned use of the direct Claude API, its server-side web search and the Batches API. What is the best next step?
options: Present legal with industry examples of companies using the direct API, to show that the constraint is stricter than necessary.
Continue with the current design so the timeline holds, and work through the legal concern during the security review.
Treat the constraint as a filter: redesign within it, quantify the impact on features, cost and timeline, and get sign-off.
Remove the affected features from the design and note the change in the next status report.
questions.explanation: Governance constraints rule options out before other trade-offs apply. The architect's job is to redesign within the constraint and communicate the consequences transparently. Deferring (B) creates rework and risk. Arguing (A) without a business case is unproductive. Silent scope changes (D) damage trust.

questions.stem: Business users of a newly launched sales-proposal assistant send scattered complaints through email and chat, and the engineering team cannot tell which issues matter most. What feedback-loop structure do you recommend?
options: Ask users to collect feedback until the next release, then review all of it together in a single prioritization session.
Contextual in-product feedback, regular triage with owners, and fixes tracked into evals.
Send a detailed satisfaction survey each quarter covering all features of the assistant.
Have the engineering team prioritize the backlog based on the technical severity of each reported issue.
questions.explanation: Effective lifecycle feedback is captured in context (reproducible), triaged with business owners (prioritized by value) and closed into evaluations (prevents regressions). The other options lose context, delay learning or exclude the people who understand the impact.

questions.stem: You must move a production assistant to a newer model version because the current one is scheduled for retirement. The new model's outputs are slightly more concise, and some users rely on the current format. What lifecycle steps are most appropriate?
options: Switch models on the retirement date, since both versions are from the same vendor and the API is unchanged.
Ask the vendor for an extended support agreement on the current model to avoid the migration.
Keep calling the current model ID after the retirement date, since retired models remain available at reduced capacity.
Run evals, adapt prompts, notify stakeholders and roll out in stages before the retirement date.
questions.explanation: Model lifecycle management means planned migrations: evaluate, adapt, communicate, roll out in stages and finish before the deadline. Surprise switches (A) break workflows. Indefinite extensions (B) cannot be assumed. Retired models will not keep serving requests (C).

questions.stem: A contact-center director announces to the board that the new AI assistant 'will replace 80% of agents within six months.' Your pilot shows 35% of contacts fully resolved without a human, with CSAT flat. What should you do?
options: Brief the director privately with the pilot data, and propose measured targets (deflection by contact type, handle time, CSAT) for the board.
Increase automatic resolution by closing more contacts without human handoff, moving closer to the stated goal.
Present the pilot data at the next board meeting to correct the record before expectations harden.
Leave it to the director, since board communication is the business owner's responsibility, and focus on improving the system.
questions.explanation: Expectation alignment is part of the architect's role. Correcting an unsupported claim privately, with data and a constructive alternative, protects the project and the stakeholder relationship. Silence (D) lets a failure narrative form. Public contradiction (C) damages trust. Gaming the metric (B) harms customers.

questions.stem: A sponsor's only requirement for the next iteration is 'make the assistant smarter.' How should you turn this into actionable requirements?
options: Turn 'smarter' into measurable targets based on the failures that matter to the sponsor.
Expand the system prompt with more detailed instructions and examples covering common question types.
Increase the context window and retrieve more documents per question, so the assistant has more information to work with.
Upgrade to the most capable model available and report the benchmark improvement to the sponsor.
questions.explanation: Vague goals must become specific, measurable requirements grounded in observed failures; otherwise no change can be shown to succeed. Jumping to a bigger model (D), more instructions (B) or more context (C) may not address the actual problem, and their success cannot be measured against 'smarter.'

questions.stem: An executive asks: 'Our product catalog changes weekly. Should we fine-tune Claude on it so it knows our products?' What is the best explanation?
options: No change is needed, since large models are trained on public web data that includes most product catalogs.
Supply changing facts at request time via retrieval or tools; fine-tuning suits behavior, not facts.
Yes: fine-tune on the catalog weekly, which builds product knowledge into the model and avoids retrieval latency.
Fine-tune once on the full catalog and use the system prompt to list the weekly changes.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is knowledge versus behavior. Changing facts should flow in at request time, where they are current, traceable and correctable. Weekly retraining (C) is costly and always lags. Claude does not know a private catalog (A). A one-time fine-tune (D) becomes stale.

questions.stem: Three months after launch, quality has slowly degraded and nobody noticed until a customer escalation. The project team had disbanded after go-live. What lifecycle gap does this reveal?
options: No defined post-launch owner or cadence for monitoring, eval maintenance and content updates.
The model was too small for the workload, and its limitations became visible as usage grew.
Users' question patterns shifted, which no design can anticipate in advance.
The user interface encouraged vague questions, which gradually lowered answer quality.
questions.explanation: AI systems need ongoing operation: monitoring, refreshed evaluations, content upkeep and periodic reviews, with clear owners. Lifecycle planning must extend past go-live. The other options look for a technical scapegoat for an ownership gap.

questions.stem: You must present an architecture recommendation to a steering committee that includes legal, finance and engineering leaders. Which document structure is most effective?
options: A concise decision document with alternatives, costs, risks and the decisions needed.
A complete technical specification covering every component, shared the night before so the committee can review it in depth.
A high-level diagram of the chosen technologies and vendors, with a short narrative of the expected benefits.
A live demonstration of the prototype, followed by open discussion of any questions.
questions.explanation: Mixed audiences need the decision framed with alternatives, costs, risks and an explicit request, with depth available but not leading. A dense spec (B) will not be read. A technology diagram with benefits only (C) says nothing about trade-offs. A demo (D) shows capability, not the decision rationale or risk position.

questions.stem: Mid-project, the client asks that the read-only support assistant also be allowed to issue credits and modify subscriptions 'since it's already integrated.' What is the right response?
options: Decline, since support assistants should remain read-only to avoid any risk of financial errors.
Add the write tools now, since the integration and authentication already exist and the request is a small extension.
Treat it as a formal scope change: reassess the risks, update governance sign-off, then agree.
Add the tools behind a feature flag and enable them after launch once usage stabilizes.
questions.explanation: Moving from read to write changes the risk profile completely. It requires a fresh risk assessment, new controls and stakeholder approval, handled as a formal scope change. Casual addition (B, D) bypasses governance. Blanket refusal (A) ignores that write actions can be done safely with the right controls.

questions.stem: A client asks how they will know, two weeks after launch, whether a claims-intake assistant is on track to deliver value. Which TWO metrics are the best early indicators to agree on up front?
options: Total tokens consumed per week, which shows how much work the assistant is doing.
Quality and risk indicators: audited extraction accuracy on a weekly sample, escalation and not-found rates, and incidents.
Rework rate and adjuster time per claim compared with the baseline.
Adoption indicators such as weekly active users and sessions per user, which show whether staff are using it.
The number of features shipped since launch, which shows the team's delivery velocity.
questions.explanation: Early indicators should connect to the eventual business outcome (rework, time saved against the baseline) and guard against quality and risk failures. Adoption (D) shows usage, not value. Token volume (A) and features shipped (E) measure activity, not value.

questions.stem: During discovery, a business owner describes the desired assistant in detail, but frontline staff who will use it describe a different workflow and different pain points. What should you do?
options: Observe the actual workflow, then reconcile both groups' views around measurable outcomes and record open conflicts.
Follow the business owner's description, since they sponsor the project and are accountable for its outcomes.
Follow the frontline staff's description, since they will use the system daily and know the real workflow.
Design two variants of the assistant, one for each group's workflow, and let usage decide.
questions.explanation: Requirements gathering must surface and resolve conflicting perspectives using evidence. Siding with one group (B, C) risks building the wrong thing or losing sponsorship. Two assistants (D) doubles cost without resolving the disagreement.

questions.stem: After a model upgrade, users report that the assistant's tone became more formal. Accuracy improved on all evaluations. Some stakeholders want to roll back. How should you handle it?
options: Keep the new model and treat the complaints as an adjustment period, since every evaluation improved.
Add a formality setting so each user can choose the tone they prefer.
Weigh both measurably, try a targeted tone fix, and decide on agreed criteria.
Roll back to the previous model, since user satisfaction is the primary measure of success.
questions.explanation: Lifecycle decisions should weigh measured trade-offs against agreed criteria, and often a targeted fix keeps the gains while addressing the concern. Rolling back reflexively (D) loses real improvements. Ignoring users (A) erodes adoption. Unevaluated settings (B) add untested variants.

questions.stem: A team's CLAUDE.md says 'Always run the linter and formatter before finishing.' Code from Claude Code sessions still occasionally arrives in PRs with lint errors. What change gives a reliable guarantee in the developer workflow?
options: Add PostToolUse and Stop hooks that run the linter, with CI as the final merge gate.
Package the lint procedure as a Skill, so Claude loads detailed linting instructions whenever it edits code.
Require plan mode for every task, so the plan always includes a linting step that the developer approves.
Strengthen the CLAUDE.md instruction with the exact lint commands, an example of a clean run, and a note that unlinted code will be rejected.
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is guidance; hooks run deterministically at defined points in Claude Code's lifecycle, and CI enforces the standard at merge regardless of who wrote the code. Emphasis (D), Skills (B) and plan mode (C) remain guidance-level and do not guarantee that lint runs.

questions.stem: In a monorepo, test files live next to the code they test throughout hundreds of folders (for example src/**/foo.test.ts). The team wants testing conventions applied only when Claude works on test files, without loading them for every task. What is the best configuration?
options: Add the testing conventions to the root CLAUDE.md under a 'Testing' heading, so Claude always has them available.
Create a 'tests' Skill containing the conventions, and ask developers to invoke it when writing tests.
Create a rule file in .claude/rules/ (for example testing.md) whose paths frontmatter lists globs such as '**/*.test.ts'.
Create a CLAUDE.md in a top-level tests/ folder containing the conventions, which Claude loads when it works on tests.
questions.explanation: Path-scoped rules match by glob, so they cover file types scattered across the repository and load only when relevant. Root CLAUDE.md (A) loads always. A folder CLAUDE.md (D) only covers that one folder. A manually invoked Skill (B) depends on people remembering to use it.

questions.stem: A CI job runs Claude Code to review every pull request and post findings as a comment. The job sometimes hangs, and on other runners it behaves differently because of developers' personal hooks and plugins on shared images. Which invocation pattern addresses both problems?
options: Run claude -p --bare with explicit settings, scoped --allowedTools, JSON output and exit codes.
Run claude in an interactive session inside tmux on the runner, with a script that sends the review prompt and captures the output.
Copy a reference developer's ~/.claude directory onto every runner, so all runners share the same hooks and plugins.
Run claude -p with --dangerously-skip-permissions, so the job never stops to ask for approval.
questions.explanation: Print mode runs once and exits, so nothing waits for input. Bare mode gives the same result on every machine by not loading whatever happens to be configured locally. Explicit tool approval, JSON output and exit codes make the job scriptable and safe. Interactive sessions (B) can hang. Skipping all permissions (D) removes safety. Copying personal configuration (C) adds variability.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants one Claude Code policy (allowed MCP servers, deny rules for secrets) for most engineers, but a stricter policy for the payments team. They plan to use server-managed settings in the Claude.ai admin console for both. What limitation should you flag, and how do you work around it?
options: Managed settings can be overridden by project settings, so the payments team should commit a stricter .claude/settings.json in their repos.
The console can't target groups yet; deploy the stricter policy via MDM or a managed file.
No limitation: the admin console supports separate managed policies per group, assigned through the identity provider.
Ask the payments team to add the stricter rules to their user settings, with periodic checks by the security team.
questions.explanation: Claude Code's documentation notes that the console applies one policy to everyone it reaches and cannot target groups yet, while file and MDM delivery can target specific machines. Managed settings cannot be overridden by users (A). User settings (D) are not enforcement.

questions.stem: Thirty repositories each have copied versions of the same Claude Code skills, subagents and hooks, and they have drifted. What is the best way to share and update them centrally?
options: Assign one owner per repository to keep its copies in sync with a shared reference document.
Consolidate all skills, subagents and hooks into one comprehensive CLAUDE.md that every repository includes.
Package them as a plugin in a team marketplace and register that marketplace for everyone through managed settings.
A scheduled job that copies a reference .claude folder into all 30 repositories each night, opening a PR when anything changed.
questions.explanation: Plugins and marketplaces are the distribution mechanism for shared Claude Code capabilities: update once and every consumer gets the change, while repository-specific guidance stays local. Copy scripts (D) create churn and conflicts. A giant CLAUDE.md (B) loads everything every session. Per-team copies (A) are the current drift problem.

questions.stem: During a long debugging session in a large repository, Claude Code's responses degrade after it has read dozens of large log files and source files. What is the most effective way to continue?
options: Use subagents for exploration, compact or restart with a summary, and keep a notes file.
Re-paste the most important log excerpts so they are recent in the conversation and easier for Claude to focus on.
Switch to a model with a larger context window and continue in the same session with all files still loaded.
Continue in the same session but ask Claude to focus only on the most recent files it read.
questions.explanation: Context hygiene keeps sessions effective: subagents isolate exploratory reading, compaction or a fresh session with a handoff clears clutter, and persistent notes preserve what matters. Re-pasting logs (B) makes it worse. A bigger window (C) postpones the problem and still dilutes attention.

questions.stem: A nightly job runs claude -p 'Update the dependency pins and run the tests'. Logs show that Bash commands for the package manager and the test runner were denied and the run finished without changes. No permission mode or allow rules were configured. Why, and what is the fix?
options: The model judged dependency updates to be risky and declined; rephrase the prompt to explain that the change is approved.
The run exceeded its output budget; raise max output tokens so the commands can complete.
Unattended runs deny any call that needs approval; pre-approve the exact commands needed with --allowedTools.
Print mode does not support Bash commands; run the task in an interactive session on a scheduled machine instead.
questions.explanation: With no one present, anything that would prompt is denied unless rules, hooks or a permission mode resolve it, so unattended runs must declare what is allowed. Bash is supported in print mode (D). The denial came from the permission system, not a model refusal (A). Token limits (B) are unrelated.

questions.stem: An engineer must refactor an unfamiliar authentication module that touches many files, and the security team wants to review the approach before any code changes. Which Claude Code workflow fits best?
options: Use print mode to generate a single patch file for security to review before applying.
Have Claude implement the refactor on a branch, then revert if security objects to the approach.
Plan mode: explore and draft a plan without edits, have it reviewed, then implement it.
Run with acceptEdits so changes are made quickly, then have security review the full diff before merging.
questions.explanation: Plan mode is designed for exploring unfamiliar code and reviewing the approach of large or sensitive changes before any edits. Reviewing only after edits (B, D) skips the requested pre-change review. A one-shot patch (A) gives no interactive planning or approval step.

questions.stem: A developer added personal permission tweaks and a local MCP server with a test token to .claude/settings.json and committed it, so teammates received both. How should Claude Code configuration be split?
options: Keep everything in .claude/settings.json and document which entries are personal, so teammates can remove what they don't need.
Move all configuration into CLAUDE.md, which is easier to read and review than JSON settings.
Keep the token in .claude/settings.json but make the repository private, so only team members can see it.
Commit shared settings in .claude/settings.json, keep personal overrides in .claude/settings.local.json, and reference secrets through environment variables.
questions.explanation: Claude Code's layering separates shared project configuration, personal project overrides and personal global settings, and secrets stay out of version control. Making the repository private (C) does not make committed secrets safe. CLAUDE.md (B) is for instructions, not settings.

questions.stem: An on-call team wants Claude Code to help investigate production incidents by reading logs, metrics and recent deploy history. What is the safest effective setup?
options: Give Claude Code production admin credentials during incidents, so it can investigate and apply fixes without delay.
Export recent production database snapshots into the session, so Claude can analyze the data directly.
Provide read-only access through scoped tools or MCP servers for logs, metrics and deploy history, keeping remediation with humans or behind approval.
Turn off permission prompts for the on-call team's sessions, so investigations are not slowed down.
questions.explanation: Operational support benefits from fast, broad read access, while changes during incidents carry high risk. Read-only scoped access with human-controlled remediation and an audit trail gives speed without new failure modes. Admin credentials (A) and disabled prompts (D) remove safety under pressure. Database dumps (B) expose sensitive data unnecessarily.

questions.stem: A production outage has three competing theories: a bad deploy, a database lock, and an expired certificate. You want three Claude Code workers to investigate in parallel and to challenge each other's findings as they go, not just report back separately at the end. Which setup fits?
options: Subagents, one per theory, each reporting its conclusion back to the main session when it finishes.
An agent team, where the teammates share a task list and message each other directly as they work.
A single session that works through the three theories one after another and compares them.
A dynamic workflow that runs one agent per log file and merges all the findings in a script.
questions.explanation: Agent teams let teammates message each other directly and challenge each other's conclusions while they work, which is exactly what competing-hypothesis debugging needs (B). Subagents only report back to the main session, so they can't debate each other (A). A single session loses the parallelism (C). A dynamic workflow runs isolated agents under a fixed script, and those agents don't talk to each other (D).

questions.stem: A team must check 600 API route files for a missing authorization check, then double-check every finding before it goes into a report. The same check applies to every file. Which approach fits best?
options: An agent team of five teammates who split up the files and talk through their results with each other.
A single session that reads all 600 files into one long context and lists the problems it finds.
A dynamic workflow that runs one agent per file, then a separate verification pass on each finding.
One subagent that reviews all 600 files on its own and returns a short summary of the problems.
questions.explanation: This is the same check repeated many times in parallel, with verification built in, which is what dynamic workflows are for: a script fans out one agent per file and then verifies each finding (C). An agent team suits a few workers who need to debate, not hundreds of identical checks, and costs more (A). One long context or one subagent would overload a single context window and miss files (B, D).

questions.stem: An orchestrator sends 100 documents to subagents. Each subagent returns a verdict, a synthesis step adds up the verdicts it received, and then every flagged document is archived automatically. Some subagents occasionally time out and return nothing. Which TWO changes fix the most serious defects?
options: Have the synthesis step compare the verdicts it received against the 100 inputs and report any that are missing.
Require human approval, or use a reversible soft-archive, before any document is actually archived.
Switch the synthesis step to a larger model so it summarizes the returned verdicts more accurately.
Double the number of subagents so each one handles fewer documents and finishes sooner.
Remove the shared trace ID from the subagent calls to cut down on logging overhead.
questions.explanation: Today a timed-out subagent silently disappears, and the report still looks complete. Comparing results against the input list makes the gaps visible (A). Archiving is irreversible and happens automatically on possibly incomplete data, so it needs a human gate or a reversible version (B). A bigger model doesn't notice missing inputs (C), more subagents don't fix silent failures (D), and the trace ID is good practice that helps debugging (E).

questions.stem: A consulting firm wants an assistant that answers questions about its own proprietary methodologies. These methodologies were never published, so they are not in the model's training data. Which AI property is the main constraint, and what is the standard mitigation?
options: Steerability: write a longer system prompt that describes each methodology in general terms.
Knowledge: retrieve the relevant methodology documents into the context at the time of each question.
Working memory: switch to a model with a larger context window so it remembers more of the firm's work.
Next token prediction: lower the temperature so the model guesses less when it answers questions.
questions.explanation: The model can't know content it was never trained on, which is a knowledge limit. The fix is to supply that content at question time through retrieval (B). A general description in the prompt is too thin and can't cover detailed questions (A). A bigger context window doesn't create knowledge the model never had (C). Lowering temperature doesn't add missing facts (D).
